title: Jingle Bells
about: James Lord Pierpont published this song in Boston in 1857, under the title One Horse Open Sleigh. It tells of a fast ride through the snow in a sleigh pulled by one horse. The song never mentions Christmas, yet it became one of the best known Christmas songs in the world.
funFact: In 1965, two astronauts played Jingle Bells in space, on a small harmonica and a handful of bells.

practice.text: Play the right hand alone, slowly, and let the song wait for each note.
Play bars 5 to 8 with the right hand alone, where the tune climbs to F.
Put both hands together. The left hand holds one low note in each bar.
Play the whole song with both hands at full speed.

tips.text: Short, short, long: the third E lasts two beats, like the jingle of a bell.
Each finger has its own key here: thumb on C, little finger on G.
Slow down a little on the last notes, and let the low C ring.

tricky.text: Finger 4 plays F three times, while the left little finger reaches down to the low F.
The F's come back. Keep finger 4 on F, and drop the left little finger to the low F again.
Finger 5 plays G twice, then fingers 4 and 2 walk down, ready for the thumb's last C.

practice.text: Tap the rhythm of bar 3 on the lid, then play the right hand alone.
Play the left hand alone, and keep each chord until the next one.
Join the hands on bars 5 to 8, where the quick notes are.
Play the whole song with both hands, a little slower than written.
Now play it at full speed.

tips.text: Long, short: the C takes a beat and a half, and the D sneaks in after it.
The last two E's are eighths. Think of one beat split in two.
Play the left hand's bass note a little louder than the chord after it.

tricky.text: Four F's with finger 4: the last one is quick, so it almost bumps into bar 6.
The F's return. Let finger 4 bounce on F, and count the short last one.
Your left little finger slides back up from B to C, as the tune starts again.

practice.text: Play the Alberti bass alone until it rolls by itself: low, high, middle, high.
Play the right hand's thirds and sixths alone, and keep both notes of each pair together.
Join the hands on the first four bars, slowly.
Play the whole song with both hands at three quarters speed.
Now play it at full speed, with the pedal.

tips.text: Keep the Alberti bass soft, so the bells of the tune ring above it.
The tune is the top note of each pair, so let the upper finger lead.
Change the pedal in the middle of each bar, as the left hand starts its pattern again.

tricky.text: Lift both hands after the D, then land on the last chord with the left hand in octaves.
On beat two, the sixth becomes a third: the thumb leaves A, and fingers 2 and 4 take C and E.
After the third, the hand runs down G, F, E and D with fingers 5, 4, 3 and 2.

practice.text: Play the stride bass alone: jump down for the bass note, then back up for the chord.
Play the right hand's chords alone, and let the little finger sing the tune.
Play the sixteenth runs of bars 9 to 12 with the right hand alone.
Join the hands on the whole song at three quarters speed.
Now play it at full speed, and make the last chord ring.

tips.text: In stride, look at the bass note and let the hand find the chord by feel.
Play the top note of each chord a little louder than the others.
Each run fits in one beat: four quick notes, then the bell rings again.

tricky.text: The tune dips from E to D over a held G and B. Finger 4 takes the D.
Spread the hand for four notes at once: G, B, F and G. Let the little finger sing.
On beat two, the thumb and little finger step down one key, while finger 2 stays on C.
